about: Numbers and news for laporteweathernow.com/amazon (Amazon Rainforest Watch). Updated weekly from official data as reported by trusted outlets. Only numbers the sources state; calm, factual, no hype. species: new-to-science discoveries in and around the Amazon (only photos with a free license, credited).
headline: Brazil's yearly forest loss is at a record low and the Rio Negro at Manaus has stopped falling, but fire smoke still hangs over parts of the lower Amazon after Lula won the Oct. 25 runoff.

stats.label: Forest cleared, Brazilian Amazon, Aug. 2025–July 2026
stats.note: Down 41.8% from 5,731 km² a year earlier and the lowest since records began in 1988 (INPE PRODES, preliminary estimate; the final rate comes in the first half of 2027).

stats.label: Amazonas towns in a drought emergency
stats.note: Amazonas state declared the emergency starting Sept. 21, citing below-average rain and the strong El Niño.

stats.label: Operations against illegal mining in Yanomami land, July–Oct. 2026
stats.note: Teams disabled or seized 10 aircraft, destroyed 15 hidden airstrips and seized 92.8 kg of mercury; the estimated loss to illegal miners was R$67 million.

stats.label: Brazil's Oct. 25 presidential runoff
stats.note: President Lula won a fourth term over Flávio Bolsonaro, by about 4.4 million votes, after Bolsonaro led the Oct. 4 first round.

now.title: Fire smoke covers Parintins again
now.text: Thick smoke from fires in the Lower Amazonas region covered Parintins, pushing fine particles above 300 micrograms per cubic meter, according to the Selva app. City schools suspended in-person classes and the federal university UFAM moved classes online. More than 30 firefighters, Ibama brigade members and National Force agents, with six firefighting planes, are working on fires that have burned for about a month in the rural Vila Amazônia area.

now.title: Four months of operations against mining in Yanomami land
now.text: Brazil's government reports 1,391 operations against illegal mining in Yanomami Indigenous Territory, Roraima, from July to October. Teams disabled six aircraft, seized four more and destroyed 15 hidden airstrips, 67 camps and 14 dredge rafts, and seized about 8.8 tonnes of cassiterite ore and 92.8 kg of mercury. The estimated loss to the illegal mining was R$67 million.

now.title: Peru destroys mining gear worth S/8.2 million in Madre de Dios
now.text: Peru's armed forces, supporting the national police, destroyed illegal mining equipment and supplies worth S/8,246,650 in the Balata area of Inambari district, Tambopata province, the Defense Ministry said. The items included 13 dredge rafts, 18 motors, 16 camps and 2,250 gallons of fuel. Prosecutors and the protected-areas service Sernamp took part.

now.title: Amazonas had its fourth-worst October for fires
now.text: INPE counted 2,271 fire detections in Amazonas state in October, behind only October 2009, 2023 and 2024. From January through October the state had 8,528, 87% more than all of 2025, which had the fewest fires in 25 years of monitoring. Environment Minister João Paulo Capobianco said the government will improve monitoring and pursue those who set fires.

now.title: Rio Negro stops falling at Manaus
now.text: The Rio Negro at Manaus held at 16.50 meters from Oct. 30 through Nov. 3, according to Port of Manaus data, after dropping 11.99 meters from its July 3 peak of 28.49 meters. The Geological Service of Brazil notes that in 91% of past years the low-water season ended in October or November. Last year the river started rising again on Nov. 12.

species.name: Two new howler monkeys, including the Mato Grosso red howler
species.where: Southern Amazonia between the Madeira and Teles Pires rivers, Mato Grosso, Brazil (A. matogrossensis); the Pantepui highlands (A. iroi)
species.text: A study of the genomes of 11 howler monkey species found two that science had not recognized. They are the first new howlers described since 1941. The Mato Grosso red howler had been counted as the Purus red howler, and it lives in one of the world's fastest-deforesting regions, so the authors say it needs an urgent assessment and may qualify as Critically Endangered. Big rivers like the Amazon, Rio Branco and Xingu kept howler populations apart for a very long time.

species.name: A hoverfly that looks like a stingless bee
species.where: Lowland rainforest in Napo Province, Ecuadorian Amazon
species.text: A fly about 12 to 14 millimeters long that mimics Trigona stingless bees, with long antennae, thick brushy hind legs and a bee-like belly. It flies low in a zig-zag. It is known from two sites about 35 kilometers apart, and the study gives the genus its first DNA barcodes.

species.name: Vivid orange killifish
species.where: Forest pools and streams of the Rio Cajari area, Amapá, Brazilian Amazon
species.text: A tiny fish, under 3 centimeters long, whose males have rows of bright orange spots and bars on pale gray sides. Its name, laranja, is Portuguese for orange. It lives in small forest pools, and like some of its relatives its eggs can wait in damp mud until the rains return. It is known from only three sites, all touched by deforestation, mining or pollution, so the scientists recommend listing it as Endangered.

species.name: Tilcayo tiger cat
species.where: Bolivia's Yungas cloud forests, where the Andes drop into the Amazon basin
species.text: The first new wild cat species named in more than 100 years. About the size of a small house cat (roughly 3 pounds), with large, irregular rosettes on light brown fur. It had been mistaken for the northern tiger cat until scientists compared the genomes of 38 wild cats. Its name is the one cloud-forest communities already used for it. Deforestation, habitat loss, disease and wildlife trafficking threaten it, and no one knows yet how many are left.

photo.alt: A small spotted wild cat, the tilcayo tiger cat, looking toward the camera

species.name: A new rain frog of flooded forests
species.where: Upper Juruá River, western Acre, Brazil
species.text: A small frog that looks almost exactly like its relatives. Scientists from UNESP and UFMG told it apart by its DNA, its slow, short mating call and small body details. It lives only in seasonally flooded forest, and the researchers warn that changing flood patterns could wipe out species like it before they are even named.

species.name: Two antbirds told apart by their songs
species.where: Amazon basin, on opposite sides of big rivers like the Amazon, Madeira and Tapajós
species.text: They look nearly identical, but they sing very differently. Brazilian scientists used an AI sound tool (BirdNET) along with feather and body measurements to show they are separate species. One is named for the Mura people of the western Amazon; the other's name means "raspy sound" for its two-note call. Naming them is the first step to protecting them.
